newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Holzmann finds break-even with new accounts. [CORRECTED 15:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Holzmann finds break-even with new accounts. [CORRECTED 15:05 GMT]

text.p: Germany's largest construction firm, Philipp Holzmann, said on Thursday it returned to break-even in 1996 after huge losses the year before, but only by realising group assets that until now lay hidden.

New accounting practices introduced by chief financial officer Rainer Klee, who joined the group only last May after 1995's disastrous losses, helped to cancel out one billion marks ($590 million) of one-off restructuring and other charges booked in 1996.
The new methods allow the group among other things to derive a gain from work which is unfinished or unbilled for. They also mean the group can revalue assets which it plans to sell in the near-term.
Klee, defending the change, told a news briefing that the accounting methods were perfectly legal and said the company had cleared the move with its auditors.
Construction stock analysts gave the new system a cautious welcome before a briefing by the company later on Thursday.

"German construction companies have had hidden reserves for some time and it is not unusual in itself if they get used, but we shall have to see more of the details," said one analyst who did not want to be identified.
Holzmann shares, buoyed by a promise from chief executive Lothar Mayer to seek to restore dividends next year, gained 39 marks to 511 in bourse trade, but with volumes relatively low.
Holzmann reported group net profit for 1996 at a bare one million marks compared to the 443 million marks of losses run up in 1995 following huge write-downs for losses on real estate projects.

The picture was less rosy at the operating level, with some 300 million marks of losses. Klee calculated this would have resulted in a loss per share of 60-70 marks according to the widely-used German DVFA standard, compared with a profit of 8.50 marks (corrects from loss) the year before.

With 1.044 billion marks of charges booked by Holzmann last year, included 464.7 million marks on the restructuring and revaluation of project development business, Holzmann's bottom-line loss would normally have soared even above 1995 levels.

But sales of assets -- such as the group's head office in a lease-back deal -- boosted its profit-and-loss account by 300.4 million marks. A further 290.4 million marks came in as a result of sales of apartments that the group had on its books.
The largest additional surplus came from a revaluation both of reserves the group is planning to sell and of the worth to the company of work for which it had not yet billed.

The latter, the company noted in its newly-published 1996 annual report, was achieved by including an "appropriate part" of management costs associated with such projects as capitalised production costs.
This allows them to be recognised as an asset.
Such revaluations all together amounted to a gain of 431.7 million marks at the construction group, Klee said.
Mayer said the 1996 results marked a new start for the company which in recent years had suffered from a period of virtually unprecedented recession in most of its major markets.
"I've been with Holzmann for the last 38 years and I can honestly say the last two have been the toughest," said Mayer, adding that he planned to step down from the company in 1998.

First quarter sales rose 10 percent to 2.7 billion marks and Mayer forecast that despite continued sluggishness in its traditional and domestic markets, the operating profit for 1997 as a whole would be significantly better.

Mayer said the group expected by around October a decision by European Commission competition authorities on whether to allow a planned cooperation between it and Hochtief AG, the country's second largest builder.
